questions.label: Problem 1
questions.statement: Design a combinatorial circuit that computes the successor function: given a binary input x between 0 and 15, output the binary numeral for x + 1. Start from the three basic logic gates; you may define and reuse boxed circuits (e.g. XOR, half-adder) along the way.

questions.label: Problem 2
questions.statement: Design a combinatorial circuit that computes x + 2: given a binary input x between 0 and 15, output the binary numeral for x + 2. Build it from the basic gates and/or boxed circuits you have already defined (e.g. the half-adder from the +1 problem).

questions.label: Problem 3
questions.statement: Design a CC that computes x + 3: given a binary input x between 0 and 15, output the binary numeral for x + 3. A good strategy is to compose circuits you have already built — e.g. feed the output of your +1 circuit into a +2 circuit (boxed sub-circuits may be chained).

questions.label: Problem 4
questions.statement: Design a combinatorial circuit that computes doubling: given a binary input x between 0 and 15, output the binary numeral for 2x. Think about what doubling does to a binary numeral’s digits.

questions.label: Problem 5
questions.statement: Design a combinatorial circuit that computes 2x + 1: given a binary input x between 0 and 15, output the binary numeral for 2x + 1. Consider how this circuit relates to your 2x circuit.

questions.label: Problem 6
questions.statement: Design a combinatorial circuit that computes 2(x+1): given a binary input x between 0 and 15 (IN1 = most significant bit), output the binary numeral for 2(x+1) (OUT1 = most significant bit). Only use ONE sub-part which computes +1 — box your +1 circuit once and reuse it, rather than incrementing twice.

questions.label: Problem 7
questions.statement: Design a combinatorial circuit that computes binary addition: given two binary inputs x and y, each between 0 and 15, output the binary numeral for x + y. Use the grade-school long-addition algorithm: work column by column, and remember the carry digit — each column really adds twice (top digit + bottom digit, then + the carry in). Reference: Petzold (2000), "A binary adding machine."

questions.label: Problem 8
questions.statement: For any integer n, in principle, could you design a CC that computes +1 [0-n] B? Why or why not? Short paragraph.

questions.label: Problem 9
questions.statement: Could you design a CC that computes +1 B (i.e. unbounded)? Why or why not? Short paragraph.

questions.label: Problem 10
questions.statement: Edge detector. Design a machine (8 inputs, 1 output) that outputs 1 iff there is a string of at least three consecutive 1s anywhere in the input.

questions.label: Problem 11
questions.statement: Object detector. Design a machine (8 inputs, 1 output) that outputs 1 iff there is a string of exactly three consecutive 1s anywhere in the input.

questions.label: Problem 12
questions.statement: Landmark recognition. Design a machine (9 inputs, 1 output) that outputs 1 iff the input = 110010111.

questions.label: Problem 13
questions.statement: Spiral. The turbot starts at the outer end of a one-cell-wide spiral corridor, facing along it, and the goal lies at the corridor’s inner end. Build a combinatorial-circuit brain that drives the turbot around the spiral and over the goal. Navigation is complete when the turbot crosses the goal cell — it does not need to stop there.

questions.label: Problem 14
questions.statement: Full circle. The turbot sits inside a walled rectangular room with no obstacles, on the bottom row of open cells, facing along the wall — and the goal lies in the cell directly behind it. Build a combinatorial-circuit brain that drives the turbot one full lap around the inside of the room and back over the goal. Navigation is completed when the turbot crosses over the goal — it does not need to stop on it. (Think of Pac-Man.)

questions.label: Problem 15
questions.statement: Zig-zag. The turbot starts at the bottom of a Z-shaped corridor, facing along its first leg; the goal lies at the far end, past two turns in opposite directions. Navigation is completed the moment the turbot crosses over the goal cell — it does not need to stop on it. Can this course be completed by a combinatorial circuit embedded in a turbot? If so, give the circuit. If not, explain why in a short paragraph.

questions.label: Problem 16
questions.statement: Representational systems. Suppose you were designing a calculator for solving a high-stakes problem. (Perhaps "you" are Nature, the "calculator" is the Brain, and the "problem" is Survival.) Would you design it to calculate in binary or in tally? Why? Use specific examples to justify your answer. ~1 paragraph.

questions.label: Problem 17
questions.statement: Embodied computation. Consider a Turbot like the one in problem 12 (landmark recognition). What function, if any, does it compute? If it does compute a function, what are the arguments and what is the value of this function? How does this compare to the function computed by the "directions" mode in Google Maps? ~1 paragraph.
